La enfermedad del Ébola es causada por un grupo de virus conocidos como ortoebolavirus. The Office for Environmental Protection said Daera had not complied with environmental law requiring it to classify and update Special Protection Areas (SPAs). Environment Minister Andrew Muir said their findings made for "uncomfortable reading". SPAs are home to rare and threatened birds like the curlew and whooper swan, which continue to decline in Northern Ireland. The OEP said action had not been taken to maintain or restore wild bird populations and their habitats. The director of RSPB NI, Joanne Sherwood, said the findings were "no surprise" and called for urgent action. Daera has two months to respond. Search Twitter YouTube Facebook Instagram Flickr LinkedIn Dalton Highway | Alaska View Map In Full Screen The Dalton Highway stretches 414 miles across northern Alaska from Livengood (84 miles north of Fairbanks) to Deadhorse and the oilfields of Prudhoe Bay. Built to allow for construction of the trans-Alaska oil pipeline in the 1970s, this mostly gravel highway travels through rolling, forested hills, across the Yukon River and Arctic Circle, through the rugged Brooks Range, and over the North Slope to the Arctic Ocean. The BLM manages a swath of public lands along the highway from the Yukon River to the north side of the Brooks Range. Within the Dalton corridor, the BLM maintains campgrounds, rest areas, interpretive panels and the Arctic Interagency Visitor Center in Coldfoot. To learn more, visit the Arctic Interagency Visitor Center website . Know Before You Go This is no ordinary road -- it pays to be prepared. The road is narrow, rough, steep, and mostly gravel -- prone to clouds of dust, slick mud, and sudden potholes. Similar to (and parallel to) the equator, the Arctic Circle is an imaginary line that geographers use to refer to a key characteristic of earth's rotation. It circles the northern hemisphere at a latitude of about 66½ degrees north. This latitude is important because it demarcates the southernmost boundary of a region -- the Arctic -- in which every location receives a full 24 hours of sunlight for at least one day of the year (summer solstice) and a full 24 hours without the sun rising above the horizon for at least one day of the year (winter solstice). Why 66½ degrees? Another way to think of it is 90 degrees north latitude (the North Pole) minus 23½ degrees = 66½ degrees. Okay, where does the 23½ degrees come from? Every day, the earth rotates around its axis. (The north pole marks one end of earth's axis of rotation. The south pole marks the other. The equator is halfway in between.) Dan Byers Dan Byers is Deputy Assistant Secretary (DAS) for Europe, Eurasia, Africa, and the Middle East at the U.S. Department of Energy’s Office of International Affairs. He is responsible for building trusted relationships to strengthen energy diplomacy and advance American interests through strategic and commercial partnerships in these regions. In this role, he leads the development and execution of regional energy strategies that expand opportunities for American energy technologies and companies while advancing broader U.S. economic and national security objectives. Prior to joining DOE, he was vice president for policy at the U.S. Chamber of Commerce Global Energy Institute, leading business community engagement and coalition building related to domestic and international energy and environmental issues. Before joining the Chamber, Byers was staff director of the Energy and Environment Subcommittee for the U.S. House of Representatives Committee on Science, Space, and Technology. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites. https://www.nist.gov/nist-and-nobel/dan-shechtman NIST and The Nobel Dan Shechtman 2011 Nobel Prize in Chemistry Credit: Alex Fine/NIST Dan Shechtman received the 2011 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for discovering crystal structures previously unknown to science: quasicrystals. Quasicrystals have transformed scientists’ understanding of how matter can arrange itself and opened scientists’ minds to a whole new class of materials that can exist. At NIST, Shechtman worked on identifying new materials that could be useful to industry, as part of NIST’s mission under the U.S. Department of Commerce. His study, sponsored by the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, was designed to develop aluminum-transition metal alloys for aerospace applications. In the process, he made a discovery that revolutionized scientific thinking. Though Shechtman worked for nearly his entire career at the Technion – Israel Institute of Technology in Haifa, Israel, he made his Nobel-winning discovery in 1982 while on a two-year sabbatical at NIST. pages.text: Dark sky tourism is on the rise across the U.S. | National Geographic By Cassandra Brooklyn Last updated April 19, 2022 • 14 min read In West Texas, Big Bend National Park is known for craggy canyons, rugged hiking trails, and its namesake bend in the Rio Grande. This month, the national park’s lustrous night skies sparked a new superlative: Big Bend became part of the largest dark sky area in the world. Clocking in at over nine million acres, the Greater Big Bend International Dark Sky Reserve , which spans West Texas and Northern Mexico , joins the 195 sites around the world certified by the International Dark-Sky Association (IDA) and the more than 60 protected dark sky areas in the United States. Many of America’s 63 national parks are dark sky areas, but only 12 are certified by the IDA. These include Grand Canyon , Mesa Verde , Joshua Tree , Death Valley , and Big Bend National Parks . Dark sky areas—parks, communities, and reserves—safeguard true wilderness conditions vital for space research and local ecosystems. They are reminders of the critical importance of protecting public lands, day and night. EBSA discloses originally submitted Form 5500 data collected through the EFAST systems as well as two Research Files that have undergone further refinement: the Private Pension Plan Research File and the Group Health Plans Research File. The Private Pension Plan Research File supports analysis of the plan, participant, and financial characteristics of the private pension plan universe and is used to produce the Private Pension Plan Bulletins Abstract of Form 5500 Annual Reports, an annual publication that summarizes data on private pension plans. The Group Health Plans Research File supports analysis of the plan, participant, and financial characteristics of the private group health plans that are required to file a Form 5500. The Group Health Plans Research File is used to produce the Group Health Plans Report, an annual publication that summarizes data on group health plans by plan funding status. Dave Chisenhall Dave Chisenhall serves as the acting director of Business Operations for the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) Office of Legacy Management (LM). He provides executive leadership and oversight of the organization’s business operations, supporting LM’s mission through strategic planning, operational excellence, organizational performance, and responsible stewardship of public resources. As director, Chisenhall leads the business operations that enable mission execution across LM’s nationwide portfolio. He oversees business process improvement, enterprise modernization, executive decision support, organizational planning, performance management, and resource management. Chisenhall works closely with DOE senior leadership to strengthen organizational effectiveness, improve operational performance, and advance the Department’s strategic priorities. Chisenhall has more than 34 years of experience in program, construction, and project management in the federal government. He served 25 years as a U.S. Air Force civil engineer officer, where he planned, programmed, designed, and managed numerous facility and infrastructure projects throughout the United States and in overseas contingency environments, filling multiple leadership roles.

pages.title: David Bushnell's 'Turtle' Was the World's First Combat Submarine
pages.description: David Bushnell developed the "Turtle" submersible as a student at Yale University. The vessel's attack on a British flagship failed, but the trailblazing boat's legacy endures 250 years later
pages.text: David Bushnell's 'Turtle' Was the World's First Combat Submarine Skip to main content America's 250th Anniversary A Smithsonian magazine special report A diagram of David Bushnell's Turtle submersible Library of Congress Prints and Photographs Division During the American Revolution, the Turtle made history as the world’s first combat-ready submarine. If all went according to plan, the driver of the acorn-shaped submersible—constructed out of oak and iron hoops—would descend, draw close enough to a warship to attach a bomb to its hull and then make their escape by ascending to the surface. Connecticut inventor David Bushnell designed the Turtle as a secret weapon for the patriots to wield against the British. Nearly 250 years ago, on the night of September 6-7, 1776, the vessel targeted the Royal Navy’s flagship, the HMS Eagle —and failed. In the centuries since, however, the story of the souped-up submersible that went up against the greatest navy in the world has served as a testament to the revolutionary spirit. Bushnell started experimenting with gunpowder while enrolled at Yale University in New Haven, Connecticut. He knew that a bomb affixed to a ship’s hull would inflict more damage than one placed on its deck. First, he had to figure out how to get explosives to work underwater. Then he would turn to the question of how to transport the device. David Denton Chief of Staff and Deputy Assistant Secretary, Technical Assistance (Acting) for OE David Denton serves as Chief of Staff and Acting Deputy Assistant Secretary for the U.S. Department of Energy’s Office of Electricity (OE), where he provides executive leadership, strategic direction, and operational oversight in support of the nation’s electric grid reliability, resilience, and security. Mr. Denton brings more than 20 years of experience in executive leadership, engineering, and infrastructure development. Prior to joining OE, he held senior leadership positions with the U.S. Department of the Interior’s Bureau of Reclamation, where he led an organization of more than 600 employees. His career also includes overseeing major energy and infrastructure projects at the Department of Energy’s Hanford Site and leading complex hydropower initiatives across the Northwest. pages.text: Death of a Family Member | U.S. Department of Labor Skip to main content Death of a Family Member When an employee covered under an employer-sponsored health plan dies, the covered spouse and dependent children need to consider their options for health coverage. If the spouse has an employer health plan available at work, the spouse and any dependents may be eligible to special enroll in that plan. Or, they may be able to special enroll in health coverage through the Marketplace. The spouse and any dependent children also may be eligible to continue their existing health coverage for up to 36 months. The plan should notify them of their right to purchase extended health care coverage under COBRA. Most plans require eligible individuals to make their COBRA election of coverage within 60 days of the plan's notice. The premature death of a spouse can undermine efforts for the partner to save for retirement, particularly if there are dependent children. That's why it's important to check your Social Security statement to find out how much children will receive if a parent dies. Maintaining adequate life insurance is also important. Be sure that you have properly named the beneficiaries for any insurance policies, retirement plans, IRAs, and other retirement vehicles. Hunters, anglers and other visitors could reach the area on foot, but the nearest available parking was nearly two miles away. Census results have several high profile applications: they are used to reapportion seats in the House of Representatives, to realign congressional districts, and as a factor in the formulas that distribute trillions of dollars in federal funds each year. This section follows the evolution of the decennial census by detailing the events surrounding each of them. pages.text: Decennial Census of Population and Housing Data Decennial Census of Population and Housing Data Skip Navigation Within Data Decennial Census of Population and Housing Data The data collected by the decennial census have changed over the decades. In 1790, each household provided the name of head of family and the number of persons in each household in five categories. By Census 2000, the short-form asked 7 questions of all residents, while the long-form added 26 population and 20 housing questions for about one in every six households. In 2005, the American Community Survey (ACS) replaced the long-form, which allowed the 2010 Census to ask just 10 questions about each person. pages.text: Decennial Census P.L. 94-171 Redistricting Data Decennial Census P.L. 94-171 Redistricting Data Skip Navigation Within About Decennial Census P.L. 94-171 Redistricting Data November 29, 2023 Written by: The Redistricting and Voting Rights Data Office (contact [email protected] or 301-763-4039) P.L. 94-171 Redistricting Data Public Law (P.L.) 94-171, enacted by Congress in December 1975, requires the Census Bureau to provide states the opportunity to identify the small area geography for which they need data in order to conduct legislative redistricting. The law also requires the U.S. Census Bureau to furnish tabulations of population to each state, including for those small areas the states have identified, within one year of Census day. Since the first Census Redistricting Data Program, conducted as part of the 1980 census, the U.S. Census Bureau has included summaries for the major race groups specified by the Statistical Programs and Standards Office of the U.S. Office of Management and Budget (OMB) in Directive 15 (as issued in 1977 and revised in 1997). Originally, the tabulation groups included White, Black, American Indian/Alaska Native, and Asian/Pacific Islander, plus “some other race.” These race data were also cross-tabulated by Hispanic/Non-Hispanic origin. At the request of the state legislatures and the Department of Justice, for the 1990 Census Redistricting Data Program, voting age (18 years old and over) was added to the cross-tabulation of race and Hispanic origin. Declaring a National Emergency to Secure the United States Bulk-Power System Executive Order Banner Color Light Text on a Dark Overlay (Default) On August 26, 2026, President Trump issued an executive order on “ Declaring a National Emergency to Secure the United States Bulk-Power System .” Executive Order 14421 declares a national emergency to protect the U.S. bulk-power system from security threats associated with foreign-supplied electrical equipment and technology. The order cites risks such as digital backdoors, malicious remote access, cyber exploitation, and supply chain vulnerabilities, amplified by the growing energy demands of artificial intelligence, data centers, and advanced manufacturing. The order authorizes the U.S. Secretary of Energy to prohibit certain acquisitions, imports, transfers, or installations of foreign-produced bulk-power system electric equipment initiated after August 26, 2026, when the Secretary makes the findings required by the order, including that the equipment has a Covered Foreign Entity nexus and presents an undue or unacceptable national-security risk. Enlarge this image Courtesy of Deepa Shivaram Courtesy of Deepa Shivaram Deepa Shivaram White House Correspondent, Washington Desk Deepa Shivaram has been covering the White House for NPR since 2022. She's extensively covered AI policy in the Biden and Trump administrations, economic fallout from the COVID-19 pandemic and the marathon that was the 2024 election. Her stories aim to contextualize the churn of White House politics and policy and how it impacts communities outside Washington. Shivaram joined NPR in 2021 as a digital news reporter covering breaking news in the U.S. and around the world. Her stories are wide ranging, from live coverage of the U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan, to analysis of Asian American representation in television. She got her start in journalism freelancing for the BBC in Washington and producing at NBC News, where she worked for the longest-running show on television, Meet the Press . In 2019, she was selected as a campaign embed for the network, closely following then Senator Kamala Harris, Senator Elizabeth Warren and other 2020 presidential contenders. Shivaram is a graduate of George Washington University, where she studied journalism and political science. She is an alum of several global journalism fellowship programs, including FASPE (Fellowship at Auschwitz for the Study of Professional Ethics), RIAS and the U.S.-Korea Journalism Exchange through the East West Center. pages.description: At Resurrection City, an epic 1968 demonstration on the National Mall in Washington D.C., protesters defined the next 50 years of activism
pages.text: Deeply Grieving MLK’s Death, Activists Shaped a Campaign of Hurt and Hope Skip to main content In 1968, at Resurrection City, a multicultural, multi-racial people shaped a campaign of hurt and hope out of a tumultuous year, including the war in Vietnam, and the assassinations of King and Robert F. Kennedy. NMAAHC, ©Jill Freedman Robert Houston’s eyes mist over as he recalls what it was like when he arrived to photograph the Poor People’s Campaign on the National Mall in Washington, D.C. in May of 1968. The campaign was conceived by Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. as a multicultural battle for economic justice for the nation’s poor. King had been assassinated the month before on April 4, but organizers carried on and galvanized African, Mexican and Native Americans, Puerto Ricans, Asians and poor whites from Appalachia and rural areas to descend on Washington for an epic demonstration. “It was a little scary that people were coming from the four corners of the United States. Strangers. People who didn’t know or barely knew each other and really didn’t care for each other. But the one thing they had in common was they had nowhere else to go,” says Houston, who covered the event for Life Magazine . “You were there for a purpose. . . . You had aches and pains just like everyone else. So it sort of made it bearable. But there was little trust between people only because they were strange to each other.” Houston got there two or three days before Resurrection City —a live-in demonstration with a shantytown settlement that existed for six weeks on the National Mall—was even built. Credit: Michael Skrepnick SCIENCE NOT EXACTLY ROCKET SCIENCE Deinocheirus Exposed: Meet The Body Behind the Terrible Hand By Ed Yong Published October 22, 2014 • 7 min read The original “terrible hands”. Credit: Eduard Solà For 50 years, the dinosaur was just a pair of arms. But what arms! Each was eight feet (2.4 metres) long, and ended in three eight-inch (20-centimetre) claws. You can understand why the scientists who discovered this beast called it Deinocheirus mirificus , from the Greek for “terrible hand, which is unusual”. The arms, hands, and shoulder girdle were discovered in 1965 in Mongolia’s Gobi desert, nestled within a 70-million-year-old sandstone formation. But the rest of the skeleton was missing, save for a few uninformative fragments. Palaeontologists have repeatedly ventured into the Gobi to try and find the rest of the animal, but without success. These failures have turned Deinocheirus into one of palaeontology’s most enduring mysteries. What kind of dinosaur was it? It was big, but how big? What did it eat? How did it live? No one could say. It was a riddle, wrapped in an enigma, hidden behind two gigantic arms. Now, a team of palaeontologists led by Yuong-Nam Lee from the Korea Institute of Geoscience & Mineral Resources has finally discovered two well-preserved specimens of Deinocheirus , which reveal the complete body behind those terrible hands. “These new specimens really solve the mystery once and for all,” says Stephen Brusatte from t
